analysis.one_liner: Bans sports betting nationwide unless states adopt strict federal safety standards for it.
analysis.headline: The SAFE Bet Act, which would have set national safety rules for sports betting, never got a committee vote and ended with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make sports betting illegal everywhere in the country unless a state applies for and wins federal approval to run its own regulated program. Any approved state program would have to meet strict federal rules: no credit-card deposits, limits on how much and how often people can deposit, a national list people can join to bar themselves from betting, a ban on most advertising, and checks to make sure bettors can afford what they wager. It would also order federal health agencies to track and report on gambling addiction.
analysis.who_benefits: People who bet on sports, and people at risk of gambling addiction, would gain the most. The bill would ban credit-card deposits, cap deposits at five per day, require affordability checks before large deposits, bar operators from using artificial intelligence to target individual bettors, create a national self-exclusion list, ban bets on games that already started and proposition bets on college and amateur sports, and restrict advertising to late-night slots away from live games. It would also fund a nationwide survey of problem gambling, a Surgeon General's report, and a federal surveillance system for gambling addiction. [S2]

how_it_helps.text: Bars operators from accepting deposits made with credit cards, caps deposits at five per 24 hours, and requires an affordability check — verifying deposits are no more than 30% of monthly income or passing a lending-style review — before accepting more than $1,000 in a day or $10,000 in a month from one person.

Creates a national self-exclusion list so a person can bar themselves from betting with operators in every opt-in state at once, not just one state at a time, and lets them set wager limits on themselves.

Prohibits betting on sporting events after they have started and bans proposition bets on amateur and intercollegiate sports, closing avenues for in-game and player-prop wagering that have drawn integrity and addiction concerns.

Restricts advertising to hours outside 8 a.m. to 10 p.m. and outside live game broadcasts, bans 'bonus' and 'no sweat' style promotions in ads, and prohibits ads that target problem gamblers, people with gambling disorder, or people under 21.

Bars operators from using artificial intelligence to track an individual's bets, target them with personalized offers, or create gambling products such as microbets — very small, rapid in-game wagers.

Requires operators to fund treatment for gambling disorder and education on responsible gaming, and orders federal agencies to run an annual nationwide survey of problem gambling, a Surgeon General's report, and a national gambling addiction surveillance system designed by researchers independent of the gambling industry.

analysis.who_pays: Sports betting operators and their investors would bear the cost: a default federal ban on accepting sports wagers unless their state wins federal approval for a regulated program, plus licensing, reserve, recordkeeping, and mandatory funding for addiction treatment. States that now collect tax revenue from legal sports betting would keep collecting only if they opt in and meet the federal standards; otherwise that revenue ends. Professional sports leagues would gain new power over which bets are allowed and whose data settles them, and broadcasters would lose most sportsbook advertising. [S2]

drawbacks.text: The default ban would overturn the legal sports betting markets that dozens of states have already created, wiping out state tax revenue and pushing bettors toward illegal offshore websites that offer none of the bill's protections.
The advertising rules would function as a near-total ban: ads could not run between 8 a.m. and 10 p.m. or during live games, leaving effectively only late-night slots.
Affordability checks would require operators to verify bettors' income or run loan-style underwriting, raising privacy questions about handing financial data to gambling companies.
The bill had no cosponsors and was never taken up by either committee, so there was no record of debate, negotiation, or consideration of its costs before it died.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are concrete and targeted at the practices most linked to gambling harm: credit-card-funded betting, rapid-fire depositing, AI-driven personalization, and advertising saturation during games. The national self-exclusion list and the federally funded, industry-independent research on gambling addiction fill real gaps in the current state-by-state patchwork. But the bill's design is heavy-handed: a default nationwide ban flips the burden onto every state, risks pushing bettors to unregulated offshore sites where no protections apply at all, and would eliminate state tax revenue in states that choose not to opt in. The near-total advertising ban and income-verification requirements would also draw serious legal and practical challenges. On balance it is a serious public-health response to a fast-growing industry, though a narrower version could have kept the strongest protections without the outright default prohibition.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the final months of the congressional session, sent to two House committees, and sat there with no cosponsors and no action until that Congress ended, which kills a bill automatically.

narrative.text: Rep. Paul Tonko introduced the bill on September 12, 2024, near the end of the two-year congressional session.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor, leaving the bill with zero cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Natural Resources committees; neither took any recorded action on it before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sports betting operators are better off because nothing changed: no federal ban, no advertising limits, no deposit caps, and no mandated addiction-treatment funding took effect. States continue to write their own, generally looser rules.

for.name: Rep. Paul Tonko
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; no other member signed on before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025, leaving it without cosponsors or committee action.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.role: House committee with a secondary referral
against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill after receiving a referral for provisions in its jurisdiction.

against.name: Sports betting operators
against.what_they_did: The fast-growing legal sports betting industry, including major online sportsbooks, had a large financial stake in avoiding federal restrictions; its opposition to federal betting mandates was widely reported around the bill's introduction.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill's only recorded support was its single Democratic sponsor, with zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill's default rule would outlaw accepting sports wagers nationwide, letting operators keep working only in states that opt into a federally approved, heavily regulated program. Deposit limits, an advertising blackout from 8 a.m. to 10 p.m. and during live games, a ban on AI-targeted promotions, and required funding for addiction treatment would all cut into a business model built on high-frequency, heavily advertised mobile betting.

The bill would bar advertising between 8 a.m. and 10 p.m. and during live game broadcasts, and would prohibit 'bonus' and 'no sweat' promotions in ads — removing most of the airtime and promotional spending sportsbooks buy from broadcasters and media companies.

Leagues would gain the right to request restrictions on bets touching their events and, for wagers placed through the end of 2024, would be the exclusive licensed source of the data used to settle them. A consumer-protection bill would hand them more control over the betting market around their games.

The bill would subject tribal operators to the same federal standards, but it also codifies that an online wager counts as occurring where the server sits, letting tribes on whose lands servers are located keep online betting revenue under tribal-state compacts.
